card.title: Principles of biotechnology — recombinant DNA technology

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The principles are genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering used together. DNA is isolated, cut, ligated into a vector, moved into a competent host and selected. The cells are then grown without contamination and the product is purified. The host is chosen to match the protein, which is why some products suit E. coli and others need mammalian cells.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Two ideas: genetic engineering (change the DNA) + bioprocess engineering (grow the cells and recover the product).
Pipeline: isolate DNA → cut → ligate into a vector → transfer into a competent host → select → scale up → downstream processing.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Genetic engineering is not the whole of biotechnology in this chapter. Growing and purifying are the second idea.  ·  Sterile does not mean 'no living cells'. It means no cells other than the production strain.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Keep EcoRI details for the tools note. This note is the reason the tools are used.  ·  Say 'competent host' when you reach the transfer step.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Human insulin genes in E. coli, followed by fermentation and purification, give a therapeutic protein.  ·  A glycoprotein that bacteria cannot decorate correctly is moved into cultured mammalian cells instead.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: E. coli is not the right host for every human protein. Glycoproteins often need animal cells.  ·  Downstream processing is not the same step as ligation. Ligation builds the DNA. Downstream processing collects the product.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Write the pipeline from isolated DNA to a purified product.  ·  Explain in four lines why insulin production needs both principles.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Engineer the gene. Then engineer the process.  ·  Sterile means only the wanted microbe, not an empty tank.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Why is a sterile fermenter part of the principle and not only a factory detail?  ·  When would you refuse E. coli as the host?

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Open a 'principles' answer with the two ideas, then the pipeline. Do not start with EcoRI unless the question asks for tools.  ·  Mention downstream processing. Answers that stop at 'the bacteria make it' are incomplete.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Genetic engineering  ·  Bioprocess engineering  ·  Sterile culture  ·  Host choice

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Two ideas: change the DNA, then culture and recover the product.  ·  Sterile culture keeps competitors out of the fermenter.  ·  Sequence: isolate, cut, ligate, transfer, select.  ·  Host choice depends on the product. Bacteria suit some proteins, mammalian cells suit others.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: An origin of replication on the vector is what lets the foreign DNA be copied as the host divides.  ·  Purification is required because the broth contains many proteins besides the one that was wanted.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What is the difference between ligation and purification?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A fermenter of the production strain is ruined if a faster contaminant takes over the sugars.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The two ideas of this chapter are → B  ·  Downstream processing means → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Biotechnology in this chapter rests on two ideas used together. Genetic engineering changes the genetic material so a cell can make something it did not make before. Bioprocess engineering grows that cell in large, clean cultures and recovers the product.  ·  A changed gene in a test tube is not yet a medicine. The host has to be multiplied without contamination, and the protein has to be separated from thousands of other molecules. Sterile culture is part of the principle, not a side comment. One unwanted microbe can outgrow the production strain.  ·  The genetic-engineering sequence is: isolate the DNA, cut out the wanted piece with a restriction enzyme, join it to a vector with ligase, put the recombinant vector into a host, and select the cells that received it. Each step fails for a different reason, so each has its own check.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Downstream processing  ·  Downstream processing separates and purifies the product.  ·  Insulin shows a product that bacteria can make. Do not generalise that every human protein is made the same way.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Selection happens before scale-up. You do not fill a fermenter with untested cells.  ·  A gene is useful at industrial scale only when the host can be grown and the product cleaned.  ·  Contamination is a failed batch, because the wrong microbe spends the nutrients.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Selection after gene transfer is what identifies the cells worth scaling up.  ·  State the two ideas and give one sentence on why both are required for insulin.  ·  List the genetic-engineering steps in order.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain what downstream processing adds after fermentation.  ·  The host must be competent, able to take DNA in. For a product that needs human-like sugar chains, a bacterial host may be the wrong choice even if it grows fast. Insulin can be made in E. coli. Some other human proteins need mammalian cells. The host is chosen for the product, not from habit.  ·  Downstream processing is the recovery half of bioprocess engineering. Cells are separated from the broth, the product is extracted, and it is purified until it is safe to use. A culture that made the protein but was never purified has not finished the process.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The same recombinant molecule can be copied only because the vector has an origin of replication and the culture is kept free of competitors. Genetic engineering supplies the instruction. Bioprocess engineering supplies the mass of cells and the clean product. Neither idea alone is the technology.  ·  # Principles of biotechnology — recombinant DNA technology ## 1.
